opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the fact that latency is really the user experience. When you're interacting with an AI model, whether it's a chatbot, a coding assistant, or an agent working through a multi-step task, every second you wait is friction. And people have very little tolerance for friction. We've seen this play out over and over in the history of computing: faster page loads, faster search results, and engagement goes up. AI is no different. It's actually more pronounced.

The second piece is that the nature of inference is changing. A year or two ago, most people were asking a model a question and getting a single answer back. Now we're moving into a world of reasoning models and agentic workflows, where one user request might trigger dozens or even hundreds of model calls behind the scenes. If each of those calls is slow, the latency compounds, and suddenly a task that should take seconds takes minutes. So low latency stops being a nice-to-have. It becomes the thing that determines whether the application is usable at all.

And then there's the economic angle. For enterprises, time is money in a very literal sense. If you have a developer using a coding assistant, and that assistant responds three times faster, that's real productivity. If you have a customer service agent powered by AI, faster responses mean happier customers and more conversations handled per hour. So when a business looks at the premium they're paying for low-latency inference, they're comparing it against the value it unlocks, and in many cases that math works out very clearly in favor of paying for speed.

So I'd say it's a combination: better experience, new use cases that only work if the system is fast, and a clear return on investment. That's why we believe inference, and specifically fast, efficient inference, is where a huge amount of the value in AI is going to be created over the next decade.

r002.rationale: It says faster page loads increase engagement and that AI is no different, connecting lower latency with users staying engaged.

r003.rationale: It describes user interactions where waiting creates friction and makes applications less usable, then connects the value of that speed to paying a premium for low-latency inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, latency is really the difference between AI being a tool you consult and AI being something you actually work with. When you're waiting three, five, ten seconds for a response, you context-switch. You go check your email, you lose your train of thought. The model becomes a batch process. But when the response comes back in a couple hundred milliseconds, it feels like a conversation, and that changes how much you use it and what you're willing to trust it with.

And the economics follow from that. If you look at where the real value is getting created right now, it's increasingly agentic workloads, where a model isn't answering one question but making a chain of calls, maybe dozens or hundreds of them, to complete a task. Every one of those hops adds latency. If each step takes two seconds, a hundred-step task is minutes. If each step takes a hundred milliseconds, it's done before you've finished your coffee. So latency doesn't just improve the experience, it determines whether an entire class of applications is even viable.

There's also a very practical angle for enterprises. Think about customer service, trading, fraud detection, anything where a human or a system is waiting on the other end. In those settings, time is literally money. A customer who waits drops off. A trade that executes late loses its edge. People have always paid for speed in those domains, and inference is no different. They're not paying for tokens, they're paying for outcomes, and faster outcomes are worth more.

And I'd add one more thing. The first wave of this industry was all about training, about how big a model you could build. But training is a one-time cost, and inference is forever. Every query, every day, for every user. So the question shifts from "how smart is the model" to "how fast and how cheaply can I actually deliver that intelligence to someone." That's where the premium for low latency comes from. People have figured out that the model's capability only matters if it shows up when you need it.

r002.rationale: It says responses in a couple hundred milliseconds feel conversational and change how much users use the AI, supporting continued engagement.

r003.rationale: It links low latency’s conversational feel and increased use to users’ willingness to pay a premium for inference.

Because latency directly affects the experience. When you’re talking to an AI assistant, you want it to feel like a conversation. If you have to wait several seconds after every question, it breaks that flow. A faster response makes the product more useful, and that’s something people will pay for.

The same applies to businesses. If an AI system helps an employee complete a task faster, or responds to a customer while they’re still engaged, there’s economic value in that speed. So the question isn’t simply, “What’s the cost per token?” It’s, “What can I accomplish, and how quickly?”

And in a business workflow, that waiting time has a cost. If faster inference lets someone complete more work, serve more customers, or make a decision sooner, paying a premium can make economic sense. So users aren’t simply paying for speed—they’re paying for what that speed enables.
